Hipposcarus harid, commonly referred to as the Candelamoa parrotfish, displays distinctive life-history traits that reflect its ecological role on coral reefs. Field surveys indicate that the ultimate total length attained by this species reaches 75 centimeters [Li = 75 centimeters], a size that places it among the medium-bodied members of the Scarinae subfamily. Newly hatched individuals emerge from the pelagic egg at a remarkably small size, with the wet weight at birth estimated at 0.00023 grams [Wwb = 0.00023 grams], a value derived from the typical egg diameter observed in related chaetodontid taxa. This minuscule starting mass necessitates a period of rapid larval growth within the planktonic community before individuals are capable of benthic settlement and the transition to a juvenile, algae-grazing lifestyle. Observations of early development in congeneric species suggest that the yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous reserves until the mouth opens and first exogenous feeding commences, a critical nutritional switch that determines survivorship during the pelagic larval phase.

As individuals progress through the post-settlement juvenile stage, a key milestone is the attainment of puberty, which in this species occurs when the total length reaches 35 centimeters [Lp = 35 centimeters]. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is calculated to be 526 grams [Wwp = 526 grams], representing a substantial increase of several orders of magnitude from the larval mass at hatching. This pronounced size gain reflects the energetic investment in somatic growth that precedes the onset of gonad maturation and reproductive activation. Individuals that have reached this developmental threshold then undergo the hormonal changes associated with the HPG axis activation, transitioning from immature, non-breeding fish to sexually mature adults capable of participating in the annual spawning aggregations that characterize many parrotfish populations. The length-based maturity schedule places the Candelamoa parrotfish in an intermediate position relative to other scarids, with a size at puberty that is roughly 47 percent of the species' ultimate length.

The maximum body size achieved by adult individuals represents a fundamental constraint on reproductive output and competitive ability. The ultimate wet weight for Hipposcarus harid is estimated at 5100 grams [Wwi = 5100 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions fitted to field-collected specimens across the species' geographic range. This asymptotic mass corresponds to the heaviest individuals recorded in survey data, typically representing large, dominant terminal-phase males that have undergone the characteristic sex change and colouration shift common among protogynous scarine fishes. Comparisons with other parrotfish species indicate that this mass is consistent with the body plan of an intermediate-sized grazer that feeds predominantly on the epilithic algal matrix, a dietary niche that requires sustained daily foraging effort to meet basal maintenance requirements and support the energetic costs of gamete production during the spawning season.

For Candelamoa parrotfish, the gonadosomatic index (GSI) measured under field conditions at a water temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C] averaged approximately 12% [GSI = approximately 12%]. The index was calculated based on gravid females captured during the peak of the reproductive season, whose ovaries exhibited advanced vitellogenic oocytes indicative of imminent spawning. The thermal environment plays a critical role in modulating this investment, as the timing of gametogenesis and the frequency of spawning bouts are tightly linked to seasonal temperature cycles that synchronise reproductive activity across the population.

Longevity data for Hipposcarus harid indicate a maximum lifespan of 4015 days [am = 4015 days] when individuals are maintained under ambient thermal conditions averaging 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C]. This estimate, equivalent to approximately 11 years, represents the oldest individuals documented from mark-recapture studies conducted in protected reef systems where fishing pressure is minimal. The lifespan places the Candelamoa parrotfish within the range of longevities reported for other medium-bodied labrids and scarids, whose survival schedules are influenced by both natural mortality from predation and the physiological costs of repeated reproduction over successive seasons. Senescence in older individuals is typically marked by a decline in body condition and a reduction in the efficiency of scale formation and fin regeneration, eventually culminating in natural mortality when physiological homeostasis can no longer be maintained. Comparative analyses suggest that the combination of a moderately long lifespan and a relatively early age at puberty allows this species to achieve multiple reproductive bouts across its lifetime, contributing to population resilience in the face of environmental variability.
